name: Sol
etymology_summary: From the Puerta del Sol, one of Madrid's medieval fortress gates during the 1520 Comuneros revolt. The gate may have had a sun carved on it, or faced east toward the sunrise.

name: Gran Via
etymology_summary: Named after the Gran Via boulevard ('Great Way'), Madrid's iconic avenue built 1910-1929 by demolishing hundreds of old buildings to create a grand east-west thoroughfare.

name: Tirso de Molina
etymology_summary: Named after Fray Gabriel Tellez (1579-1648), known by his pen name Tirso de Molina, a Mercedarian friar and playwright who created the character of Don Juan in 'El burlador de Sevilla'.

name: La Latina
etymology_summary: Named after Beatriz Galindo 'La Latina' (1465-1534), a humanist and Latin scholar who served as tutor and advisor to Queen Isabel la Catolica.

name: Goya
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco de Goya (1746-1828), the great Spanish painter and printmaker. The street and plaza were named first; the station follows.

name: Arguelles
etymology_summary: Named after Agustin de Arguelles (1776-1844), a liberal lawyer and politician of the Cortes of Cadiz, known as 'El Divino' for his oratory.

name: Chueca
etymology_summary: Named after Federico Chueca (1846-1908), composer of the genero chico zarzuela, a form of Spanish light opera. His most famous work is 'La Gran Via'.

name: Embajadores
etymology_summary: From 'embajadores' (ambassadors). Foreign ambassadors fleeing a plague outbreak under King Juan II (15th century) took refuge outside the city walls here.

name: Lavapies
etymology_summary: Disputed: (1) From a fountain where Jews washed their feet ('lava pies') before entering the synagogue; (2) From Manzanares river mud. Most cite the Jewish quarter connection.

name: Chamberi
etymology_summary: Named after the neighbourhood/district. See district entry for etymology (disputed, linked to Chambery, Savoy). This station closed in 1966 and reopened as a museum ('Estacion Fantasma') in 2008.

name: Callao
etymology_summary: Named after the plaza, which commemorates the 1866 naval Battle of Callao against Peru.

name: Opera
etymology_summary: Named after the nearby Teatro Real (Royal Opera House), inaugurated in 1850.

name: Principe de Vergara
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Baldomero Espartero (1793-1879), military leader who was regent and prince of Vergara after the Convention of Vergara (1839).

name: Alfonso XIII
etymology_summary: Named after King Alfonso XIII (1886-1941), who inaugurated and helped fund the first Metro line in 1919.

name: Gregorio Maranon
etymology_summary: Named after Gregorio Maranon y Posadillo (1887-1960), physician, scientist, historian, and precursor of endocrinology in Spain.

name: Paco de Lucia
etymology_summary: Named after Paco de Lucia (1947-2014), the legendary flamenco guitarist who revolutionized the genre and brought it international recognition.

name: Manuela Malasana
etymology_summary: Named after Manuela Malasana (1791-1808), a young seamstress killed resisting French troops on May 2, 1808. A symbol of Madrid's popular resistance against Napoleon.

name: Principe Pio
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco Pio de Saboya (1659-1726), Italian aristocrat and military commander who supported Felipe V during the War of Spanish Succession. His palace stood nearby.

name: Eugenia de Montijo
etymology_summary: Named after Eugenia de Montijo (1826-1920), Countess of Teba and Empress of France as wife of Napoleon III.

name: Guzman el Bueno
etymology_summary: Named after Alfonso Perez de Guzman 'el Bueno' (1256-1309), military strategist who famously defended Tarifa against the Moors, choosing duty over his own son's life.

name: Alonso Martinez
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel Alonso Martinez (1827-1891), jurist and politician who authored the 1888 Spanish Civil Code.

name: Diego de Leon
etymology_summary: Named after Diego de Leon (1807-1841), a military officer and politician executed for his role in a failed pronunciamiento.

name: Vicente Aleixandre
etymology_summary: Named after Vicente Aleixandre (1898-1984), poet of the Generation of '27 who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1977. Station renamed in 2018 (formerly Metropolitano).

name: Concha Espina
etymology_summary: Named after Concha Espina (1869-1955), a prominent Spanish novelist.

name: Santiago Bernabeu
etymology_summary: Named after Santiago Bernabeu (1895-1978), long-serving president of Real Madrid football club. The station was renamed from 'Lima' in 1997 due to its proximity to the stadium.

name: Estacion del Arte
etymology_summary: Renamed in 2018 to reflect the station's position at the heart of Madrid's art triangle: Museo del Prado, Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, and Museo Reina Sofia.

name: Feria de Madrid
etymology_summary: Renamed from 'Campo de las Naciones' in 2017 due to proximity to the IFEMA trade fair complex.

name: Estadio Metropolitano
etymology_summary: Renamed from 'Estadio Olimpico' in 2017 when Atletico Madrid moved to the Wanda Metropolitano stadium nearby.

name: Atocha
etymology_summary: Named after the Atocha railway station, which takes its name from 'atocha' (esparto grass, Stipa tenacissima) that grew abundantly in the area.

name: Piramides
etymology_summary: Named after two obelisk-pyramids (14m high) built in 1831 by architect Francisco Javier de Marietegui at the entrance to Puente de Toledo. They still stand today.

name: Tribunal
etymology_summary: Named after the Tribunal de Cuentas (Court of Auditors), built in 1863, located on the street above. Originally called Hospicio after the nearby Royal Hospice orphanage (1726).

name: Noviciado
etymology_summary: Named after the Jesuit novitiate (Noviciado de la Compania de Jesus) that stood on Calle San Bernardo. The building later became the Universidad Central.

name: Bilbao
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta de Bilbao roundabout, which honours the Basque city of Bilbao. The glorieta was a historic boundary point of northern Madrid.

name: Quevedo
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta de Quevedo, honouring Francisco de Quevedo (1580-1645), one of Spain's greatest Golden Age poets and satirists.

name: Islas Filipinas
etymology_summary: Named after the Philippine Islands (Islas Filipinas), former Spanish colony. The nearby Avenida de Filipinas was named to honour the archipelago's colonial connection to Spain.

name: Moncloa
etymology_summary: Named after the Moncloa area. The name derives from 'Mons Clovis' (Latin for Mount of Clovis), referencing the Frankish king. Linked to the Castillo de la Monclova estate in Seville.

name: Ventas
etymology_summary: Named after Las Ventas, the area where the famous Plaza de Toros de Las Ventas bullring (1931) is located. 'Ventas' refers to the roadside inns that once dotted this area.

name: Manuel Becerra
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel Becerra Bermudez (1820-1896), mathematician, engineer, and politician who served as minister under Amadeo I and Alfonso XII. He was also Grand Master of the Grand Orient of Spain.

name: O'Donnell
etymology_summary: Named after Calle O'Donnell, honouring Leopoldo O'Donnell (1809-1867), 1st Duke of Tetuan, general and prime minister of Spain. The street was named when Madrid's walls were torn down in 1868.

name: Ibiza
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Ibiza, which references the Balearic island of Ibiza. The street naming is linked to the Dukes of Medinaceli who held properties on the island.

name: Pacifico
etymology_summary: Named after the former Calle del Pacifico (now Avenida de la Ciudad de Barcelona), which honoured the Spanish Navy's victories on the Pacific coast of Chile and Peru in 1865-1866.
named_after: Spanish naval campaigns in the Pacific (1865)

name: Menendez Pelayo
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Menendez Pelayo, honouring Marcelino Menendez y Pelayo (1856-1912), a renowned writer, philologist, and literary critic from Santander. Nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature.

name: Rios Rosas
etymology_summary: Named after Antonio de los Rios Rosas (1812-1873), a jurist, orator, and liberal politician from Ronda (Malaga). He was one of the most respected parliamentarians of 19th-century Spain.

name: Iglesia
etymology_summary: Named after the Iglesia de Santa Teresa y Santa Isabel, a parish church built 1842-1856 near the Glorieta de Joaquin Sorolla. The station was originally planned as 'Martinez Campos'.
named_after: Iglesia de Santa Teresa y Santa Isabel
previous_names: Martinez Campos (planned but never used); Sorolla (Civil War era)

name: Cruz del Rayo
etymology_summary: Named after the Colonia Cruz del Rayo residential area. The toponym refers to a stone cross that was struck and damaged by lightning ('rayo') at some historical point.
named_after: Cruz del Rayo (stone cross struck by lightning)

name: Prosperidad
etymology_summary: Named after the Prosperidad neighbourhood, itself named for Prospero Soynard y Polen, a 19th-century landowner who parcelled the area's properties, attracting working-class immigrants from the interior.

name: Cuatro Caminos
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta de Cuatro Caminos, a crossroads where four major roads converge: Bravo Murillo, Reina Victoria, Santa Engracia, and Raimundo Fernandez Villaverde.

name: Tetuan
etymology_summary: Named after the barrio of Tetuan de las Victorias, which commemorates Spain's victory in the Battle of Tetuan (1860) during the Spanish-Moroccan War led by General O'Donnell.

name: Estrecho
etymology_summary: Named after the local area which honours the Strait of Gibraltar (Estrecho de Gibraltar), continuing the neighbourhood's North African military nomenclature theme (near Tetuan).

name: Valdeacederas
etymology_summary: Named after the historical street (now Capitan Blanco Argibay). 'Valdeacederas' means 'valley of the sorrels' (Rumex acetosa), a plant that grew abundantly in the area.

name: Francos Rodriguez
etymology_summary: Named after Jose Francos Rodriguez (1862-1931), journalist, playwright, and mayor of Madrid (1910). He was also a prominent member of the Real Academia Espanola.

name: Carpetana
etymology_summary: Named after Via Carpetana, which references the Carpetani, a pre-Roman Celtic people who inhabited central Iberia including the area of modern Madrid. Paleontological remains (14 million years old) were found during station works in 2008.

name: Oporto
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Oporto, which references the Portuguese city of Porto (Oporto in Spanish). Part of Madrid's tradition of naming streets after significant European cities.

name: Vista Alegre
etymology_summary: Named after the Vista Alegre neighbourhood, which takes its name from the Quinta de Vista Alegre ('Joyful View Estate'), a royal estate purchased by Queen Maria Cristina in 1832.

name: Carabanchel
etymology_summary: Named after the Carabanchel district, formerly two independent municipalities (Alto and Bajo). Etymology is debated: possibly from Arabic 'carab' (cultivated land owner) or 'garbanzal' (chickpea field).

name: Arturo Soria
etymology_summary: Named after Arturo Soria y Mata (1844-1920), visionary urbanist who designed the Ciudad Lineal (Linear City) concept in Madrid, a pioneering model of urban planning built 1892-1911.

name: Esperanza
etymology_summary: Named after the Esperanza housing development (colonia). The station serves the Esperanza neighbourhood in the Ciudad Lineal district.

name: Canillas
etymology_summary: Named after the historical village of Canillas, an ancient settlement annexed to Madrid in 1949. The village had an agricultural character for centuries.

name: Mar de Cristal
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta Mar de Cristal roundabout in the Hortaleza district. The poetic name 'Sea of Crystal' likely references the area's development.

name: Chamartin
etymology_summary: Named after the former municipality of Chamartin de la Rosa, annexed to Madrid in 1948. The name likely derives from an old estate or family name; the area was historically rural.

name: Colombia
etymology_summary: Named after the South American country of Colombia. Located in the Hispanoamerica neighbourhood where many streets are named after Latin American countries and locations.

name: Nuevos Ministerios
etymology_summary: Named after the Nuevos Ministerios government complex, designed by Secundino Zuazo Ugalde and sponsored by Minister Indalecio Prieto. Construction began 1933, completed 1942.

name: Ruben Dario
etymology_summary: Named after Ruben Dario (1867-1916), the Nicaraguan poet who founded the literary movement of Modernismo. Born Felix Ruben Garcia Sarmiento.

name: Nunez de Balboa
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Vasco Nunez de Balboa (1475-1519), the Spanish explorer who was the first European to sight the Pacific Ocean from the Americas in 1513.

name: Barajas
etymology_summary: Named after the district of Barajas, a former independent town annexed to Madrid. The name likely derives from a Moorish landowner 'Bar Axa' (son of Axa) or from the Arabic/Jewish hybrid name of the area's medieval lord.

name: Canillejas
etymology_summary: Named after Canillejas, an ancient village founded in the 13th century and annexed to Madrid in 1949. It served as an agricultural settlement providing water and crops to Madrid for over six centuries.

name: Torre Arias
etymology_summary: Named after the Quinta de Torre Arias, a 16th-century noble estate built during the reign of Felipe II. The tower and estate passed through several aristocratic families including the Counts of Villamor and Dukes of Osuna.

name: Legazpi
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Legazpi, honouring Miguel Lopez de Legazpi (1502-1572), the Basque conquistador who led the expedition to colonise the Philippines and became the first governor-general of the Spanish East Indies.

name: Delicias
etymology_summary: Named after the Paseo de las Delicias, originally 'las Delicias del rio' (Delights of the River). The name comes from the Palace of Delicias del Rio, a historic pleasure ground near the Manzanares River. The nearby Delicias railway station (1880) is now the Railway Museum.

name: Mendez Alvaro
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco Mendez Alvaro (1806-1883), a physician, writer, and briefly mayor of Madrid in 1843. His term lasted only one month.

name: Palos de la Frontera
etymology_summary: Named after the town of Palos de la Frontera in Huelva province, from where Columbus set sail in 1492. The station was originally called 'Palos de Moguer' due to a historical error that confused the towns of Palos de la Frontera and Moguer; corrected in 1986.

name: Pavones
etymology_summary: Named after the Pavones neighbourhood in the Moratalaz district. The station is under the Calle de la Hacienda de Pavones.

name: Valdebernardo
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdebernardo neighbourhood, a relatively recent urban development in the Vicalvaro district, officially designated as a neighbourhood in 2017.

name: Vicalvaro
etymology_summary: Named after the historic town of Vicalvaro, annexed to Madrid. The town is notable for the Pronunciamiento de Vicalvaro (1854), a military uprising led by General O'Donnell.

name: San Cipriano
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de San Cipriano, honouring Saint Cyprian, a 3rd-century Christian martyr. The saint's name derives from Latin 'Cyprianus', meaning 'from Cyprus'.

name: Hospital 12 de Octubre
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, a major public hospital. The hospital's name references October 12, Spain's National Day (Dia de la Hispanidad), commemorating Columbus's arrival in America in 1492.

name: Almendrales
etymology_summary: Named after the Almendrales neighbourhood. 'Almendrales' means 'almond groves', referencing the almond trees that historically grew in this area south of Madrid.

name: Usera
etymology_summary: Named after the Usera district, which takes its name from Colonel Marcelo Usera. He married the daughter of 'Tio Sordillo', a farmer whose lands he proposed to develop into housing plots (1925-1930).

name: Plaza Eliptica
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza Eliptica roundabout, so called because of its elliptical shape. It sits at the junction of the Usera and Carabanchel districts.

name: Puerta de Arganda
etymology_summary: Named as a gateway ('puerta') to the municipality of Arganda del Rey. The station marks the boundary where the metro exits Madrid towards Arganda.

name: Arganda del Rey
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality of Arganda del Rey. The name 'Arganda' likely derives from the Indo-European root 'arg' (white/bright). 'Del Rey' was added in 1996, referencing Philip II's 1583 purchase of the town from the Archbishopric of Toledo.

name: La Poveda
etymology_summary: Named after the La Poveda neighbourhood of Arganda del Rey. 'Poveda' derives from 'alameda' (poplar grove), referencing the poplar trees (chopos) that historically grew in this area.

name: Tres Olivos
etymology_summary: Named after the Tres Olivos residential area. 'Tres Olivos' means 'Three Olive Trees', a toponym referencing olive trees that marked the location.

name: Montecarmelo
etymology_summary: Named after the PAU (urban development) of Montecarmelo. 'Monte Carmelo' references Mount Carmel, a mountain range in Israel sacred to the Carmelite religious order.

name: Las Tablas
etymology_summary: Named after the PAU of Las Tablas, a modern residential development. 'Las Tablas' means 'The Boards/Planks', likely a rural toponym referencing flat terrain or wooden structures.

name: Pinar de Chamartin
etymology_summary: Named after the pine grove ('pinar') that was part of the former municipality of Chamartin de la Rosa. The area retains its name from the historical wooded landscape.
named_after: Pinar de Chamartin (pine grove of Chamartin)

name: Anton Martin
etymology_summary: Named after Anton Martin de Dios (1500-1553), a Spanish religious figure and nurse who founded the Hospital de San Juan de Dios at this location in 1552.

name: Retiro
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque del Buen Retiro (Park of the Pleasant Retreat), created in the 1630s as a royal pleasure ground for King Felipe IV by the Count-Duke of Olivares.

name: Banco de Espana
etymology_summary: Named after the Bank of Spain building (1891), the country's central bank, located adjacent to the station at Plaza de Cibeles.

name: Sevilla
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de Sevilla, a street referencing the Andalusian city of Seville. The station sits at the intersection of Calle de Alcala and Calle de Sevilla.

name: Santo Domingo
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Santo Domingo, which references the Dominican convent of Santo Domingo el Real that stood nearby from the 13th century until its demolition in 1869.
named_after: Convento de Santo Domingo el Real

name: San Bernardo
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de San Bernardo, which references Saint Bernard of Clairvaux. A Cistercian monastery dedicated to him once stood on this street.

name: Canal
etymology_summary: Named after the Canal de Isabel II water infrastructure. The station is near the Third Reservoir of the Canal de Isabel II, Madrid's water supply system inaugurated in 1858 under Queen Isabel II.

name: Ventura Rodriguez
etymology_summary: Named after Ventura Rodriguez Tizon (1717-1785), one of Spain's most important 18th-century architects. He worked on the Palacio Real and designed numerous churches and public buildings in Madrid.

name: Puerta de Toledo
etymology_summary: Named after the Puerta de Toledo, the last monumental gate built in Madrid (completed 1827). It was designed as a triumphal arch by Antonio Lopez Aguado, originally conceived during the Napoleonic occupation.

name: Acacias
etymology_summary: Named after the Paseo de las Acacias (Acacia Walk), a promenade lined with acacia trees in the Arganzuela district.

name: Marques de Vadillo
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco Antonio de Salcedo y Aguirre (c.1660-1729), 1st Marques de Vadillo, the corregidor (chief magistrate) of Madrid who commissioned the Puente de Toledo bridge, designed by Pedro de Ribera.
named_after: Francisco Antonio de Salcedo y Aguirre

name: Conde de Casal
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel Escriva de Romani y de la Quintana (1871-1954), Count of Casal, a lawyer, politician, senator, and ceramics historian who served in the Madrid city council.

name: Sainz de Baranda
etymology_summary: Named after Pedro Sainz de Baranda y Gorriti (1775-1855), considered Madrid's first constitutional mayor (alcalde). He led the city government during the War of Independence and the Liberal Triennium.

name: Serrano
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Serrano, honouring Francisco Serrano y Dominguez (1810-1885), regent of Spain and general. The street was named after the 1868 revolution.

name: Velazquez
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Velazquez, honouring Diego Velazquez (1599-1660), the great Spanish painter of the Baroque period, famous for 'Las Meninas'.

name: Lista
etymology_summary: Named after Alberto Lista y Aragon (1775-1848), a mathematician, poet, journalist, and literary critic from Seville. The original street name was changed to Jose Ortega y Gasset in 1955 but the station kept the name.

name: Colon
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Colon, honouring Christopher Columbus (Cristobal Colon), the explorer who reached the Americas in 1492. A 17-metre marble monument (1885) stands in the plaza.

name: Republica Argentina
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de la Republica Argentina, honouring Argentina. Part of the Hispanoamerica neighbourhood where streets are named after Latin American countries.

name: Alonso Cano
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Alonso Cano, honouring Alonso Cano (1601-1667), a painter, sculptor, and architect from Granada, known as the 'Spanish Michelangelo'.

name: Cuzco
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Cuzco, which honours the Peruvian city of Cusco (Cuzco), the historic capital of the Inca Empire. Part of the Latin American naming theme in the Hispanoamerica neighbourhood.

name: Plaza de Castilla
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Castilla, a major square at the northern end of Paseo de la Castellana. Named after the historic Crown of Castile.

name: Alvarado
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Alvarado, honouring Pedro de Alvarado (c.1485-1541), a Spanish conquistador and captain under Hernan Cortes during the conquest of Mexico and Central America.

name: Puente de Vallecas
etymology_summary: Named after the Puente de Vallecas district, which references the bridge ('puente') built over the Abroñigal stream that connected Madrid to the Vallecas area.

name: Nueva Numancia
etymology_summary: Named after the Nueva Numancia neighbourhood. In 1873 residents petitioned to declare it an independent town named 'Nueva Numancia' after the legendary Celtiberian city of Numancia that resisted Roman siege (133 BC).

name: Portazgo
etymology_summary: Named after the local area, which references a medieval 'portazgo' (road toll) on the Valencia road at Vallecas. Portazgos were taxes charged for using newly constructed roads.

name: Puerta del Angel
etymology_summary: Named after the Puerta del Angel neighbourhood. The name originates from a 1605 ermita built to house an angel figure rescued from the Puerta de Guadalajara after it burned in 1582.

name: Alto de Extremadura
etymology_summary: Named after its elevated location ('alto') along the road to Extremadura (Paseo de Extremadura), the historic route from Madrid to the Extremadura region of western Spain.

name: Lucero
etymology_summary: Named after the Lucero neighbourhood in the Latina district. 'Lucero' means 'bright star' or 'morning star' in Spanish.

name: Laguna
etymology_summary: Named after the Laguna neighbourhood. 'Laguna' means 'lagoon' or 'small lake', likely referencing a former body of water in the area.

name: Aluche
etymology_summary: Named after the Aluche neighbourhood. The name is believed to derive from the Luche stream ('Arroyo de Luche') that ran through the area. Maps noted it as 'A. Luche' (Arroyo Luche), which evolved into 'Aluche'.

name: Campamento
etymology_summary: Named after the Campamento neighbourhood, which references the military camps ('campamentos') that were established in the area. The name dates to 1885 when the mayor of Carabanchel Alto designated the area.

name: Batan
etymology_summary: Named after the Venta del Batan, a historical inn associated with the bull pens ('corrales') where fighting bulls were kept before fights. 'Batan' refers to a fulling mill.

name: Lago
etymology_summary: Named after the lake ('lago') in the Casa de Campo park, a large artificial lake near this entrance to the park.
named_after: Lago de la Casa de Campo (lake)

name: Casa de Campo
etymology_summary: Named after the Casa de Campo, Madrid's largest public park (1722 hectares). Originally a royal hunting estate acquired by Felipe II in 1562, it was opened to the public in 1931.

name: Plaza de Espana
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Espana, one of Madrid's major squares featuring monuments to Cervantes and his literary characters Don Quijote and Sancho Panza.

name: Ciudad Universitaria
etymology_summary: Named after Madrid's Ciudad Universitaria (University City), home to the Universidad Complutense de Madrid, the Polytechnic University, and UNED. The campus was planned in the 1920s under Alfonso XIII.

name: Pio XII
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Pio XII, honouring Pope Pius XII (Eugenio Pacelli, 1876-1958), who was head of the Catholic Church from 1939 to 1958.

name: Duque de Pastrana
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza Duque de Pastrana. The Duchy of Pastrana was created in 1572 by Felipe II for Ruy Gomez de Silva, Prince of Eboli. The area's naming reflects the historical presence of the ducal estate.
named_after: Ruy Gomez de Silva (1st Duke of Pastrana)

name: Herrera Oria
etymology_summary: Named after Angel Herrera Oria (1886-1968), journalist, educator, Catholic social activist, and priest. He founded the newspaper El Debate and the Catholic Association of Propagandists.

name: Barrio del Pilar
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio del Pilar neighbourhood, which references the Virgen del Pilar (Our Lady of the Pillar), one of Spain's most important Catholic devotions, patron of Zaragoza.

name: Ventilla
etymology_summary: Named after the Ventilla neighbourhood. 'Ventilla' is a diminutive of 'venta' (inn/tavern), suggesting there was a small roadside inn at this location.

name: Mirasierra
etymology_summary: Named after the Mirasierra neighbourhood, meaning 'Mountain View' - referring to the views of the Sierra de Guadarrama visible from the area. The colonia was founded c.1927-1950 as a residential development.

name: Arganzuela-Planetario
etymology_summary: Named after the Arganzuela district and the Planetario de Madrid (planetarium), located in the nearby Parque Tierno Galvan. Opened in 2007 within an already-operating line.

name: Suanzes
etymology_summary: Named after Juan Antonio Suanzes Fernandez (1891-1977), naval engineer, first president of the Instituto Nacional de Industria (INI), and Minister of Industry under Franco. He was posthumously honoured with the Marquis of Suanzes title in 1960.

name: Ciudad Lineal
etymology_summary: Named after the Ciudad Lineal district, which takes its name from Arturo Soria's pioneering 'Linear City' urban planning concept (1892-1911).

name: Quintana
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Quintana in the Ciudad Lineal district. The Quintana neighbourhood was developed as part of the broader urban expansion of eastern Madrid.

name: El Carmen
etymology_summary: Named after the El Carmen neighbourhood, which likely references the Virgen del Carmen (Our Lady of Mount Carmel), a widely venerated figure in Spanish Catholicism.

name: Garcia Noblejas
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de los Hermanos Garcia Noblejas, referencing the Garcia-Noblejas brothers, a family of five Falangist members during the Spanish Civil War. The naming is politically controversial.

name: Simancas
etymology_summary: Named after the Simancas neighbourhood, which references the Castilian town of Simancas (Valladolid), famous for the Battle of Simancas (939) and the General Archive of Simancas.

name: Las Musas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Musas neighbourhood, referencing the Muses of Greek mythology. The area was a residential colony (colonia) in the Canillejas zone with mythological and classical street names.

name: San Blas
etymology_summary: Named after the San Blas neighbourhood, honouring Saint Blaise, a 4th-century Armenian bishop and martyr who is the patron saint of throat ailments.

name: Pueblo Nuevo
etymology_summary: Named after the Pueblo Nuevo neighbourhood, meaning 'New Town'. The area developed as a new settlement on the outskirts of Madrid in the 19th-20th centuries.

name: Pinar del Rey
etymology_summary: Named after the Pinar del Rey neighbourhood, meaning 'King's Pine Grove', referencing a historical royal pine forest in the Hortaleza district.

name: Bambú
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Bambu in the Chamartin district. The street name references the bamboo plant, part of a botanical naming theme in the neighbourhood.

name: Estrella
etymology_summary: Named after the Estrella neighbourhood in the Retiro district. The station is located beneath the M-30 motorway near the Calle Estrella Polar.

name: Vinateros
etymology_summary: Named after the Camino de Vinateros, an old path used by wine merchants ('vinateros') who transported wine through this area south of Madrid.

name: Artilleros
etymology_summary: Named after the Pico de Artilleros, referencing artillerymen ('artilleros'). The military name reflects the historical presence of military installations in the area.

name: Avenida de America
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de America, a major avenue in Madrid named to honour the Americas. The station is a major multimodal transport hub.

name: Cartagena
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Cartagena, referencing the historic port city of Cartagena in the Murcia region of southeastern Spain.

name: Antonio Machado
etymology_summary: Named after Antonio Machado (1875-1939), one of Spain's greatest poets of the Generation of '98. His most famous work is 'Campos de Castilla'. He died in exile in Collioure, France.

name: Valdezarza
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdezarza neighbourhood in the Moncloa-Aravaca district. 'Valdezarza' likely derives from 'valle de zarza' (bramble valley), referencing wild blackberry bushes in the area.

name: Colonia Jardin
etymology_summary: Named after the Colonia Jardin housing development, a 'garden colony' (colonia jardin) inspired by the early 20th-century garden city movement promoting green residential spaces.

name: Opanel
etymology_summary: Named after the Opanel neighbourhood in the Carabanchel district. The origin of the name 'Opanel' is unclear but may derive from a local family name or estate.

name: Rivas Vaciamadrid
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality of Rivas-Vaciamadrid. 'Rivas' comes from Guillermo Rivas, an 11th-century military founder. 'Vaciamadrid' derives from Arabic 'Fahs al-Mayrit' (field of Madrid).

name: Julian Besteiro
etymology_summary: Named after Julian Besteiro Fernandez (1870-1940), socialist politician who served as President of the Cortes Constituyentes during the Second Republic and as president of PSOE and UGT.

name: Juan de la Cierva
etymology_summary: Named after Juan de la Cierva y Codorniu (1895-1936), the engineer from Murcia who invented the autogiro (autogyro), the precursor to the helicopter, which first flew successfully in 1923.

name: Alonso de Mendoza
etymology_summary: Named after Alonso de Mendoza, a nobleman from Getafe. Sometimes confused with the Spanish conquistador Alonso de Mendoza who founded La Paz, Bolivia in 1548.

name: Hospital Severo Ochoa
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Severo Ochoa in Leganes, which is named after Severo Ochoa de Albornoz (1905-1993), the Asturian biochemist who won the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for RNA synthesis research.

name: Reyes Catolicos
etymology_summary: Named after the Reyes Catolicos (Catholic Monarchs): Queen Isabella I of Castile (1451-1504) and King Ferdinand II of Aragon (1452-1516), who unified Spain and sponsored Columbus's voyage.
named_after: Reyes Catolicos (Isabella I and Ferdinand II)

name: Manuel de Falla
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel de Falla (1876-1946), one of Spain's most important classical composers, known for works like 'Noches en los Jardines de Espana' and 'El Amor Brujo'.

name: Marqués de la Valdavia
etymology_summary: Named after the Marques de la Valdavia, a noble title associated with the Alcobendas area. The title was held by local landowners with significant historical presence in the municipality.
